passage: It was 2 a.m. in Melbourne when Freya realised she had watched forty short videos in a row and still hadn't started her history essay. Her eyes stung. At school the next day she yawned through maths and snapped at Tuan when he asked to borrow a pen. At lunch she admitted it. "My phone's eating my nights." Tuan said his was the same. That weekend, at a party, someone passed round a vape and Freya felt the old pull to just go along; she shook her head and went to get juice instead. On Sunday she and Tuan made a deal: phones charge in the kitchen after ten, and they text each other a thumbs-up when they've done an hour of homework first. By Wednesday, she'd finished the essay.

qa.q: Where did Freya and Tuan agree their phones would charge after ten?
qa.a: In the kitchen.

qa.q: Why did Freya snap at Tuan when he asked for a pen?
qa.a: She was exhausted and irritable from staying up till 2 a.m. watching videos, and probably annoyed with herself for not starting the essay.

qa.q: Which part of their plan is most likely to help, and why?
qa.a: Charging phones in another room removes the late-night temptation, and texting each other makes it easier to keep going because someone is counting on them. 👍

qa.q: How might Tuan benefit from Freya admitting her problem?
qa.a: It lets him say he struggles too, so instead of both hiding it, they can build the habit together.

grounding: Shows a teen noticing screen overuse hurting her sleep and work, refusing a risky offer, and setting up healthier habits.

passage: Study hours in the girls' hostel ran from seven to nine, and phones were meant to stay in the warden's locker. Reena had a second phone hidden in her pillowcase. Every evening she scrolled under the blanket while Nirmala, her roommate, worked through chemistry. By the second month Reena was failing tests and sleeping through the morning bell. "Come with me to the common room," Nirmala said one night, dragging her by the wrist. She had made a timetable on chart paper: forty minutes' work, a short walk down the corridor, then another block. "I'll do it with you. If you want, give me the phone till Friday." Reena hesitated, face tight with embarrassment, then pulled it out and dropped it into Nirmala's palm. "Only till Friday," she muttered.

qa.q: Where did Reena hide her second phone?
qa.a: In her pillowcase.

qa.q: What does Reena's tight face suggest when she hands over the phone?
qa.a: She seems embarrassed that her habit has become obvious and hard to control, but also relieved someone is willing to help.

qa.q: How could the hostel warden support students like Reena?
qa.a: The warden could talk privately with her about how she's coping, and back study plans like Nirmala's rather than only punishing hidden phones.

qa.q: What is it like for Nirmala to share a room with Reena's habit?
qa.a: She has to study next to glowing screens every night and watches her friend slip, so offering the timetable is both caring and a relief for herself.

grounding: Shows a hostel teen caught in screen overuse and slacking off, and a peer helping her build study discipline.

passage:
Dear Uma didi,

You asked on the phone why I sounded different. Here's the honest version.

Till last month I was gaming till three most nights. I'd wake up late, skip breakfast, and fall asleep in the bus. My marks dropped, and I lied to Mummy that the teachers were marking harder.

Then at the colony terrace, some older boys offered me a cigarette. I almost took it just to look cool. I said no, but it scared me how close I came.

So I changed things. I made a timetable and stuck it on the cupboard. Games only on Saturday. Phone out of the room by eleven. I've started cycling in the mornings. I still slip sometimes, but I feel more awake.

Don't tell Mummy about the cigarette. I'll tell her myself.

Love,
Mahima

qa.q: Until what time was Mahima gaming most nights?
qa.a: She was gaming till three most nights.

qa.q: How did Mahima feel about nearly taking the cigarette?
qa.a: It frightened her how close she came, which shows she realised peer pressure could pull her into risks she did not want.

qa.q: What would you advise Mahima about telling her mother?
qa.a: Telling her mother herself, as she plans, is a good step; she could also admit the lie about her marks so she can get support at home.

qa.q: If you were Uma, what would you want to say back?
qa.a: That you are proud of her for noticing and changing, and glad she trusted you with the hard parts. 🤍

grounding: A teen writes about moving from late-night gaming, lies and a near-slip with a cigarette toward better time and health habits.

passage: 'Parveen, you asked why I've stopped replying at 2 am. Okay, so. In the summer holidays I was on my phone till three most nights, videos, one after another. I'd tell myself, one more, and suddenly it was light outside. School started and I was falling asleep in first period. Our class teacher actually asked, "Hafsa, is everything okay at home?" which was so embarrassing. So I made rules. Phone charges in the kitchen from ten-thirty. I bought an old alarm clock from the market for eighty rupees. The first three nights I lay there itching to check it. Now I read for a bit and I'm asleep before eleven. I'm not perfect. Sundays I still slip. But my mornings feel like mine again.'

qa.q: How much did Hafsa pay for the alarm clock?
qa.a: Eighty rupees.

qa.q: Why did Hafsa find the teacher's question embarrassing?
qa.a: It showed Hafsa's tiredness was obvious to adults, and Hafsa felt ashamed that the late nights looked like trouble at home.

qa.q: What could help Hafsa on the Sundays when Hafsa slips?
qa.a: Hafsa could keep the phone-in-the-kitchen rule on weekends too, or ask a family member for a gentle reminder.

qa.q: How might Parveen be affected by Hafsa's new routine?
qa.a: Parveen loses a late-night chat partner, but may also feel nudged to look at Parveen's own habits.

grounding: Shows a teenager replacing late-night screen use with simple rules that protect their sleep and school mornings.

passage: I'm Sudha, Kavitha's cousin, and we share a room when she stays over on weekends. This month I noticed a few things. She used to scroll in bed till late; now her phone sits on my desk after ten, and she lays out her school clothes before sleeping. Last Saturday some older boys from the colony were smoking behind the water tank and called her over. I was on the terrace and saw her shake her head, laugh, and keep walking to the shop. When she came up, she didn't mention it. She just said, 'I'm doing the morning run with Papa tomorrow, wake me at six.' I don't know if saying no was hard for her. She didn't look like it. But she did take the long way home.

qa.q: Where were the older boys smoking?
qa.a: Behind the water tank.

qa.q: What might Kavitha taking the long way home suggest?
qa.a: It may suggest she felt uneasy about the boys and wanted to avoid them, even if saying no looked easy, though Sudha can't be sure.

qa.q: How could Kavitha's family support these new habits?
qa.a: They could keep up the morning runs with Papa, notice her routines, and stay someone she can talk to if the pressure grows.

qa.q: How does Sudha seem to feel about the change in Kavitha?
qa.a: Sudha seems quietly impressed and a little curious, noticing the changes without asking directly.

grounding: Illustrates a teenager keeping healthy routines and turning away from a substance risk, seen by her cousin.

passage: Week one: Ayesha, sixteen, scrolled short videos in bed until two every night, then dragged herself to school with a headache. Her sister Preeti found her asleep over her books on Thursday. Week two: Ayesha tried a rule: phone charging in the kitchen after ten. The first night she lay awake, itchy, reaching for a phone that wasn't there. The third night she read a novel instead and fell asleep by eleven. Week four: her headaches had eased, and she'd finished two chapters of revision before breakfast. "I still miss it," she admitted to Preeti. "But I don't miss feeling like a zombie."

qa.q: Where did Ayesha charge her phone after ten?
qa.a: In the kitchen.

qa.q: What was Ayesha feeling the first night without her phone?
qa.a: She felt restless and uncomfortable, missing the habit badly.

qa.q: What made Ayesha's new rule work?
qa.a: It was simple and physical, keeping the phone out of reach, and she replaced scrolling with reading.

qa.q: How might Preeti see the change in her sister?
qa.a: Relieved and impressed that Ayesha stuck with it despite the struggle.

grounding: Shows a teenager moving from late-night screen use to a healthier routine over a month.

passage: "Hansa, you asked why I never smoked. When I, your Jatin Mama, was sixteen, the boys behind the bus depot all did, and gutka too. One evening they held out a packet to me. 'Just try, don't be a baby.' My hands were in my pockets, sweaty. I knew what it had done to my uncle's teeth and lungs. I said, 'I have football at six,' and walked away. They laughed. So I made football my excuse every day, and then it stopped being an excuse. I ran every morning for ten years. Those boys still call me 'Coach'."

qa.q: What excuse did young Jatin give when offered the packet?
qa.a: "I have football at six."

qa.q: What was young Jatin feeling with his sweaty hands in his pockets?
qa.a: He felt pressured and nervous, afraid of being mocked but determined not to start.

qa.q: What turning point in the story built Jatin's lasting habit?
qa.a: Using football as his excuse every day until it became a real routine.

qa.q: How might the boys behind the depot have seen Jatin later?
qa.a: With some respect, since they now call him "Coach".

grounding: Shows an elder recalling how as a teenager he resisted substance pressure and built a healthy habit instead.

passage: Board exams were six weeks away, and Bhupen, seventeen, was playing online games until three every night. His marks were sliding. His mother Farida didn't want a fight, so one evening she sat beside him. "How many hours today?" He shrugged. "Five? Six?" "And studying?" "One." She didn't take the phone. "Make me a plan you can actually keep." He grumbled, then wrote: two hours of games on weekends only, phone out of the room at eleven, study in forty-minute blocks. The first week he broke it twice. The second week, once. Farida noticed and said nothing, just left a plate of cut fruit by his desk.

qa.q: How many weeks away were the board exams?
qa.a: Six weeks away.

qa.q: What might Bhupen have been feeling when he admitted to five or six hours?
qa.a: Probably guilty and a bit embarrassed, knowing his marks were sliding.

qa.q: Why did Farida's approach work better than taking the phone?
qa.a: Letting Bhupen make the plan gave him ownership, so he was more likely to stick to it.

qa.q: How might Farida feel in the second week?
qa.a: Quietly relieved and hopeful as he breaks the plan less often.

grounding: Shows a teenager, with his mother's help, working to control heavy gaming under exam time pressure.

passage: At 3 a.m. in the Rohini flat, the only light was Dhruv's screen. One more match, he kept telling himself. At eight his sister Chandrika shook him awake. "You missed physics tuition. Again." Dhruv groaned. His eyes burned and his head felt stuffed with cotton. That afternoon he failed a quiz he'd have aced a month ago. On the metro home, he opened his phone and saw the number: nine hours of screen time yesterday. He felt a sick lurch. That night, at eleven, he plugged his phone in the kitchen and left it there. He lay awake, restless, reaching for a phone that wasn't there. On the third night, he fell asleep before midnight. Chandrika raised an eyebrow at breakfast. "You look human."

qa.q: Where did Dhruv plug his phone in at night?
qa.a: In the kitchen.

qa.q: What was Dhruv feeling when he saw nine hours of screen time?
qa.a: He felt shocked and uneasy, a sick lurch, realising how much gaming was costing him.

qa.q: What worked in Dhruv's plan, and what could help if the pull comes back?
qa.a: Keeping the phone out of the bedroom at eleven; he could also ask Chandrika to check in, or set a game-time limit.

qa.q: How does Chandrika see the change in her brother?
qa.a: She notices he looks rested and teases him gently, clearly relieved.

grounding: A teenager notices his late-night gaming habit harming his studies and moves his phone out of his room.

passage:
"Rekha, come outside for a minute."
"Why?"
Afreen lowered her voice. "Some of the seniors are passing around a vape by the back gate. They asked for you."
"Me?" Rekha looked toward the gate. Music thumped from the hall. "Everyone's trying it, apparently."
"Are you going to?"
"I don't know. It's just once, right?"
"That's what Nikhil said. Now he can't get through class without one. He told me it started as 'just once.'"
Rekha chewed her lip. "They'll think I'm scared."
"You are scared. So am I. That's not stupid."
Rekha laughed shakily. "Okay. Let's go get cold drinks instead and stay inside."
"And if they ask?"
"I'll say I've got football trials. Which I do."

qa.q: Where were the seniors passing around the vape?
qa.a: By the back gate.

qa.q: What was Rekha feeling when she chewed her lip?
qa.a: She felt torn and anxious, tempted to fit in but worried about the risk.

qa.q: What helped Rekha make her choice?
qa.a: Afreen's honest warning about Nikhil, and permission to admit being scared, plus a simple reason to say no.

qa.q: How might Afreen feel after Rekha decides to stay inside?
qa.a: She likely feels relieved and glad they faced the pressure together.

grounding: At a school event, a teenager is tempted by a vape but decides against it after a friend's honest warning.

passage: I'm Pankaj. Last year, in Class 11, I gave up on everything. I skipped running practice, slept till eleven on Sundays, and ate chips for dinner while scrolling. I told myself I'd start fresh "from Monday," every week. Coach Maria called me one evening and said, "You've got talent, but talent doesn't run the laps." It stung. She helped me make a boring, simple plan: lights out at eleven, run at six, homework before phone. The first week, I hated it. By the second month, I noticed I wasn't tired all the time, and my marks were climbing. I still slip up on weekends. But now when I miss a day, I start again the next morning, not "from Monday."

qa.q: What did Coach Maria say talent doesn't do?
qa.a: Talent doesn't run the laps.

qa.q: How did Pankaj feel when Coach Maria said that?
qa.a: Pankaj felt stung, hurt by the truth of it.

qa.q: What change in Pankaj's thinking helped most?
qa.a: Starting again the next morning after a slip, instead of waiting for Monday.

qa.q: How might Coach Maria see Pankaj's progress?
qa.a: She would likely feel encouraged and proud that the simple plan worked.

grounding: A teenager looks back on building discipline around sleep, exercise and study with a coach's help.

passage:
Hostel warden's note, girls' wing, Term 2
Gurleen, Class 11, has been handing in homework late for three weeks. Her roommate Elizabeth told me Gurleen watches short videos on her phone until two or three most nights and then sleeps through the morning bell.
I spoke with Gurleen on Thursday. She was defensive at first, then admitted, "I open it for five minutes and look up and it's midnight." She seemed tired and fed up with herself.
We agreed on a small plan she chose herself: phone charges at the warden's desk from eleven, alarm clock instead of phone alarm, and one hour of video on Sundays as a treat.
Elizabeth offered to study with her after dinner.
I have informed her parents and will check in with her every Monday for a month.

qa.q: Where will Gurleen's phone charge from eleven?
qa.a: At the warden's desk.

qa.q: How did Gurleen feel when she admitted how long she spent on videos?
qa.a: She felt tired and fed up with herself, after being defensive at first.

qa.q: What makes the warden's plan likely to work?
qa.a: Gurleen chose the steps herself, the plan is small and clear, and there are weekly check-ins and a study partner.

qa.q: How is Elizabeth affected by Gurleen's late nights?
qa.a: As a roommate, Elizabeth sees the problem up close and cares enough to offer to study together after dinner.

grounding: A warden's note on a teen struggling with late-night screen use and building a simple discipline plan.

passage:
Tuesday night
Neelam's older cousin offered us a vape behind the tuition centre today. Neelam took it. Everyone was watching me.
I said no. Well, I said, "Nah, my asthma," which is half true. My heart was going crazy. Nobody pushed, but a boy laughed.
On the walk home Neelam said, "It's just flavour, it's harmless." I don't think that's true, we literally did a chapter on it. But I didn't argue. I didn't want to sound like a teacher.
I told Mumma at dinner, without naming Neelam's cousin at first. She didn't shout. She thanked me, and we agreed she'd have a word with the tuition centre about who hangs around behind it.
I'm glad I said no. I'm worried about Neelam.
Sarita

qa.q: Where was the vape offered?
qa.a: Behind the tuition centre.

qa.q: What was Sarita feeling when everyone was watching?
qa.a: Sarita felt nervous and pressured; the heart was going crazy.

qa.q: Which choice worked, and what could Sarita do about Neelam?
qa.a: Saying no and telling Mumma the same day worked; Sarita can also talk to Neelam privately or ask a trusted adult to help.

qa.q: How might Neelam feel if Sarita raised it gently?
qa.a: Neelam may feel defensive at first but perhaps also relieved that a friend cares.

grounding: A teen's diary about refusing a substance offered by peers and telling a parent.

passage: In their small town near Nashik, the one bus to the junior college left at 6:40, and Nirmala had missed it twice that week. Each night she meant to sleep by ten and ended up scrolling short videos till one. On Thursday her friend Arohi found her asleep on her desk during the free period. "You look like a ghost," Arohi said. That evening Nirmala left her phone charging in the kitchen next to Aai's tiffin tins, set the old wind-up alarm clock, and wrote her study hours on a card above her bed. The first night she reached for the empty bedside table three times. By Monday she was at the bus stop at 6:30, eating a banana, and Arohi waved from the bus window.

qa.q: What time did the bus to the junior college leave?
qa.a: It left at 6:40.

qa.q: What does Nirmala reaching for the empty table three times suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt a restless pull toward the phone; the habit was strong even though she had decided to change.

qa.q: Which of Nirmala's changes made the biggest difference, and why?
qa.a: Charging the phone in the kitchen took the temptation out of the bedroom, so she slept earlier and made the bus.

qa.q: How does Arohi see Nirmala before and after the change?
qa.a: Arohi first worries that Nirmala looks like a ghost, then is glad to see Nirmala at the bus stop on time. 😊

grounding: Shows a teenager replacing late-night scrolling with simple sleep and study habits.
